definition: Encryption that uses the same secret key both to encrypt data and to decrypt it.
wrongs: Encryption that uses a public key to encrypt and a different private key to decrypt.
A one-way function that maps data to a fixed-length digest that cannot be reversed.
A filter that accepts or drops packets according to address and port rules.
why: Both parties share one secret, so that same key undoes the encryption.
example: Two office laptops share a secret key and use it to encrypt a spreadsheet before emailing it.
scenario: Alice and Bob already share a secret key. Which property lets Bob read a file Alice encrypted with that key?
scenarioAnswer: The same shared key decrypts it
scenarioWrongs: A different public key decrypts it
Any hash of the file decrypts it
scenarioWhy: Symmetric encryption decrypts with the same secret key that was used to encrypt.

definition: Encryption that uses a public key to encrypt data and the matching private key to decrypt it.
wrongs: Encryption that uses one shared secret for both encryption and decryption.
A checksum stored beside a file so accidental bit flips can be noticed.
A tunnel that hides addresses by sending all traffic through one gateway.
why: Anyone may encrypt with the published key, but only the private-key holder can decrypt.
example: A browser encrypts a short secret with a bank site's published key so only the bank can read it.
scenario: A website publishes one key and keeps another secret. Which key should visitors use to encrypt data for that site?
scenarioWrongs: A hash of the home page
scenarioWhy: Public-key encryption lets anyone encrypt to the owner with the published key.

definition: A symmetric block cipher that encrypts 128-bit blocks using a 128-, 192-, or 256-bit key.
wrongs: A public-key algorithm whose security depends on factoring a large modulus.
A hash function that outputs a 256-bit digest of any input.
A key-agreement method that derives a shared secret from public values.
why: AES is the standard symmetric block cipher used to encrypt bulk data with one shared key.
example: A disk-encryption tool uses AES-256 so a laptop drive stays unreadable without the key.
scenario: A product must encrypt large files quickly with one shared secret. Which algorithm fits that job?
scenarioWhy: AES is a symmetric block cipher built for fast bulk encryption with a shared key.

definition: A public-key algorithm whose security depends on the difficulty of factoring a large modulus.
wrongs: A symmetric block cipher that encrypts 128-bit blocks with one shared key.
A hash function used only to detect accidental file corruption.
A firewall mode that remembers a connection before allowing return traffic.
why: RSA builds a public and private key from two large primes and their product.
example: An email program encrypts a short message key with the recipient's RSA public key.
scenario: A protocol needs a public-key operation based on the hardness of integer factoring. Which algorithm matches?
scenarioWhy: RSA is the classic public-key algorithm whose trapdoor is related to factoring.

definition: A one-way function that maps data of any length to a fixed-size digest.
wrongs: A reversible cipher that restores the original file when the digest is known.
A shared-key cipher that encrypts data in fixed-size blocks.
A signed document that binds a person's name to a public key.
why: The digest has a fixed length, and the input should not be recoverable from it.
example: A download page publishes a SHA-256 digest so students can check that an installer was not altered.
scenario: A team must detect a changed file without being able to rebuild the file from the check value. What should they store?
scenarioAnswer: A cryptographic hash of the file
scenarioWrongs: An AES ciphertext of the file name only
A firewall log of the download
scenarioWhy: A cryptographic hash is a one-way fingerprint of the file contents.

definition: A value made with a private key so others can verify the signer and the data with the public key.
wrongs: A shared password both parties type before a file transfer starts.
A symmetric ciphertext that hides a message from everyone but the sender.
A rule that allows network traffic only from one named subnet.
why: Only the private-key holder can create a signature that the matching public key accepts.
example: A software vendor signs a release so customers can confirm the package came from that vendor.
scenario: Customers must confirm that a patch came from the vendor and was not edited. What should the vendor attach?
scenarioWrongs: A symmetric session key in the clear
scenarioWhy: A digital signature ties the vendor's private key to the exact bytes of the patch.

definition: A protocol that authenticates an endpoint and encrypts application data on a network connection.
wrongs: A disk layout that stores each file as blocks linked by a content hash.
A host filter that drops packets with private source addresses.
A password store that keeps only unsalted copies of user secrets.
why: After the handshake checks the server, TLS protects the confidentiality and integrity of the session data.
example: A browser shows a lock because the campus bank site finished a TLS handshake and uses HTTPS.
scenario: A web app must encrypt HTTP and let browsers check the server certificate. Which protocol should it use?
scenarioWhy: TLS is the protocol that secures web sessions and authenticates the server certificate.

definition: A control that allows or blocks network traffic according to a stated security policy.
wrongs: A cipher that encrypts every packet with a 128-bit block key.
A hash stored in a certificate so a browser can rebuild a private key.
A signature method that proves who sent an email message.
why: A firewall compares traffic with rules and then permits or denies each connection.
example: A lab server allows inbound TCP port 443 from campus and drops every other inbound connection.
scenario: An admin must permit only HTTPS into a server and reject other inbound ports. Which control does that?
scenarioWhy: A firewall rule can allow one service port and deny the remaining inbound traffic.

definition: A monitor that analyzes traffic or host activity and raises alerts about suspected attacks.
wrongs: A device that encrypts all traffic so packet contents cannot be read.
A method that agrees a shared secret between strangers with no prior key.
An authority that issues public-key certificates to named users.
why: An intrusion detection system reports suspicious events and does not by itself block them.
example: A campus sensor alerts analysts when many hosts suddenly probe the same closed port.
scenario: The team wants warnings about odd scans, while a person still decides whether to block them. What should they deploy?
scenarioWhy: A detection system raises alerts for people to review instead of automatically blocking traffic.

definition: An encrypted tunnel that carries private traffic across a shared or public network.
wrongs: A hash that replaces a password in a user database.
A list of allowed hardware addresses on a switch port.
A signature a browser checks before it runs a downloaded script.
why: The tunnel encrypts packets so outsiders on the shared network cannot read the private traffic.
example: A remote employee opens the company VPN and then reaches an internal file server as if on the office LAN.
scenario: Staff at home must reach internal servers over the internet without exposing that traffic. What should they use?
scenarioWhy: A VPN encrypts the path between the remote computer and the internal network.

definition: The authorities, policies, and certificates used to bind public keys to checked identities.
wrongs: A single shared password given to every host on a local network.
A cipher mode that encrypts each block independently of the others.
A log format that records only failed login attempts.
why: Relying parties trust a public key because a certificate authority has vouched for the binding.
example: A university authority issues certificates so campus services can trust each server's public key.
scenario: An organization must issue and revoke certificates that tie employee names to public keys. What system does that?
scenarioWhy: Public key infrastructure is the set of authorities and certificates that bind keys to identities.

definition: A key-agreement method that lets two parties derive the same shared secret over a public channel.
wrongs: A block cipher that encrypts data with a 256-bit key in 128-bit blocks.
A signature method that signs a hash with the sender's private key.
A filter that drops packets whose source address does not match the port.
why: Each side combines its own private value with the other side's public value to compute the same secret.
example: A TLS handshake uses ephemeral Diffie-Hellman so the browser and server agree a fresh session key.
scenario: Two hosts have never shared a key and must agree one while an eavesdropper can see their messages. Which method fits?
scenarioWrongs: Publishing the finished secret in the clear
Reusing a static password as the ciphertext
scenarioWhy: Diffie-Hellman derives a shared secret from public values without sending that secret.

definition: The original readable data before encryption, or the readable data restored by decryption.
wrongs: The scrambled output produced by a cipher.
The public certificate that names a server.
The rule set a firewall uses to drop packets.
why: Plaintext is the meaningful message that a cipher is meant to hide and later restore.
example: The sentence in an email is plaintext until the mail program encrypts it for the recipient.
scenario: After Bob decrypts a message with the correct key, what form is the recovered message in?
scenarioWhy: Decryption restores the original readable plaintext.

definition: The scrambled output of encryption, which hides the original message from anyone without the key.
wrongs: The original readable message before any cipher is applied.
A public key listed in a directory.
An alert written by an intrusion sensor.
why: Ciphertext should be unreadable unless the proper decryption key is applied.
example: A messaging app stores an encrypted chat blob on a server, and only the users' devices hold the keys.
scenario: An observer records the bytes leaving a laptop after encryption and before they reach the server. What are those bytes?
scenarioWhy: Encryption turns the readable message into ciphertext before it crosses the network.

definition: A symmetric cipher that encrypts fixed-size groups of bits under a secret key.
wrongs: A cipher that combines data with a keystream one byte at a time.
A one-way function that outputs a digest instead of ciphertext.
A protocol that only checks user names and never encrypts data.
why: Block ciphers such as AES work on a fixed block length rather than a continuous stream of bytes.
example: AES takes each 128-bit chunk of a database backup and encrypts that chunk under the backup key.
scenario: A designer picks a cipher that always processes 128-bit chunks with one secret key. What kind of cipher is that?
scenarioWhy: A block cipher encrypts fixed-size blocks under a symmetric key.

definition: A symmetric cipher that combines plaintext with a pseudorandom keystream, often one byte at a time.
wrongs: A cipher that encrypts data only in large fixed blocks such as 128 bits.
A public-key method that publishes a modulus and an encryption exponent.
A monitor that alerts when traffic matches a known attack pattern.
why: A keystream is generated from the key and combined with the plaintext to produce ciphertext.
example: A radio link encrypts each outgoing byte by combining it with the next byte of a keystream.
scenario: A link encrypts a continuous byte stream by combining each byte with a keystream. Which cipher type is that?
scenarioWrongs: A block cipher used only on whole files
scenarioWhy: A stream cipher encrypts a running sequence with a keystream rather than fixed blocks.

definition: A keyed tag that lets a receiver check that a message is unchanged and came from a holder of the key.
wrongs: An unkeyed digest that anyone can recompute without a secret.
A public certificate issued by a trusted organization.
A tunnel header that hides the original network addresses.
why: Only a party that knows the shared key can produce a tag the receiver will accept.
example: An API attaches a keyed tag of each request body so the server can reject a modified call.
scenario: Two servers share a secret and must notice if a status message changes in transit. What should they append?
scenarioWrongs: An unkeyed checksum anyone can forge
A second copy of the plaintext
scenarioWhy: A message authentication code uses the shared secret so an outsider cannot forge a valid tag.

definition: A unique random value stored with a password hash so identical passwords do not share the same digest.
wrongs: The secret key used to decrypt a symmetric ciphertext.
A public certificate that identifies a website.
A timer that closes idle firewall connections.
why: A different salt forces each stored hash to differ even when the passwords are the same.
example: Two students choose the same password, but the login table stores different hashes because each row has its own salt.
scenario: A login database must keep identical passwords from producing identical stored hashes. What should be mixed in before hashing?
scenarioWhy: A unique salt makes each stored password hash different even for matching passwords.

definition: An organization that checks identities and issues signed digital certificates for public keys.
wrongs: A symmetric algorithm that encrypts blocks on a disk.
A sensor that only raises alerts and never issues credentials.
A local file that stores unsalted password guesses.
why: Others trust the certificate because it was signed by an authority they already accept.
example: A browser trusts a university login site because a recognized authority signed that site's certificate.
scenario: A company wants ordinary browsers to trust its new website certificate. Who should sign that certificate?
scenarioWhy: Browsers trust a site certificate when a recognized certificate authority has signed it.

definition: A signed document that binds an identity to a public key and states a validity period.
wrongs: A shared secret used by a block cipher to encrypt a disk.
An alert record produced by a network sensor.
A random value stored beside a password hash.
why: The issuer's signature lets others rely on the name-to-key binding inside the certificate.
example: A server presents a certificate that names its domain and contains the public key browsers should use.
scenario: During a handshake the server must show which public key belongs to its domain name. What does it send?
scenarioWhy: A digital certificate binds the domain name to a public key under an issuer's signature.

definition: A property where later exposure of a long-term key does not reveal the keys of past sessions.
wrongs: A property where one stolen session key decrypts every earlier and later session.
A hash property that makes two different files share one digest.
A firewall property that allows all outbound traffic by default.
why: Each session uses an ephemeral secret that is discarded and cannot be derived from the long-term key alone.
example: A mail server uses ephemeral Diffie-Hellman so a later theft of its private key does not unlock old sessions.
scenario: Designers want a stolen long-term server key to be useless for reading recorded past sessions. Which property is that?
scenarioWrongs: Encrypting every session under a static key only
scenarioWhy: Forward secrecy keeps past session keys independent of the long-term private key.

definition: The security goal of keeping information readable only by parties allowed to see it.
wrongs: The goal of showing that data was not changed, even if everyone can read it.
The goal of keeping a service reachable during heavy demand.
The goal of proving who created a file without hiding its contents.
why: Confidentiality is about secrecy of content, usually enforced by access control or encryption.
example: A clinic encrypts patient notes so only staff with the proper keys can read the diagnoses.
scenario: A hospital must stop outsiders from reading stored lab results. Which security goal is that?
scenarioWhy: Keeping unauthorized people from reading the data is confidentiality.

definition: The security goal of detecting or preventing unauthorized changes to data.
wrongs: The goal of hiding data so unauthorized people cannot read it.
The goal of issuing public-key certificates to employees.
The goal of carrying traffic through an encrypted remote gateway.
why: Hashes, message authentication codes, and signatures provide evidence about whether data changed.
example: A backup job stores a hash beside each archive so staff can tell whether the archive was edited.
scenario: Auditors must notice if a grade file changes after the instructor saves it. Which goal are they protecting?
scenarioWhy: Noticing an unauthorized change is the integrity goal.

definition: The process of checking that a claimed identity is genuine before trusting it.
wrongs: The process of hiding a file's contents with a cipher.
The process of placing public servers on a screened subnet.
The process of compressing logs before they are archived.
why: Authentication examines evidence such as a password, key, or certificate for the claimed identity.
example: A student portal asks for a password and a phone code before it treats the session as that student.
scenario: A mail server must check that a person really is the account holder before showing the inbox. What process is that?
scenarioWhy: Authentication checks the identity claim before the server grants access.

definition: Evidence that a party cannot convincingly deny having signed or sent a particular message.
wrongs: Evidence that a packet always took the shortest network path.
Evidence that two users memorized the same symmetric password.
Evidence that a firewall dropped every inbound packet.
why: A digital signature tied to a controlled private key is evidence that the signer approved the message.
example: An online approval stores a manager's digital signature so the manager cannot later deny the purchase.
scenario: A dispute needs evidence that one specific manager approved a purchase order. Which goal supplies that evidence?
scenarioWhy: Non-repudiation gives evidence that the identified manager signed the order.

definition: A design that protects a symmetric key with public-key cryptography and encrypts the bulk data with that key.
wrongs: A design that hashes a file and treats the digest as the encrypted content.
A design that uses only packet filters and never encrypts data.
A design that signs cleartext with a shared password and sends no key.
why: Public-key operations are slower, so they wrap a short key while a symmetric cipher handles the data.
example: A mail program encrypts a letter with AES and encrypts that AES key with the recipient's RSA public key.
scenario: A large video must be encrypted quickly, yet only the recipient's private key should unlock it. Which design fits?
scenarioWrongs: Hashing the video and sending only the digest
Encrypting every video byte with RSA alone
Signing the video and sending it unencrypted
scenarioWhy: The hybrid design uses public-key encryption for a short AES key and AES for the video.

definition: A short-lived symmetric key used to protect the data of one communication session.
wrongs: A long-term private key that is published inside a certificate.
A password salt that stays in a user table for years.
A firewall rule that is configured never to expire.
why: Limiting a key to one session reduces how much data is exposed if that key later leaks.
example: After a handshake, a browser and server encrypt the page traffic with a key they discard when the session ends.
scenario: A call should be protected by a key that will not be reused for tomorrow's call. What kind of key is that?
scenarioWhy: A session key is created for one conversation and then discarded.

definition: A non-secret starting value that lets the same plaintext encrypt differently under the same key.
wrongs: The private key that must stay secret for decryption to remain safe.
A certificate serial number that identifies a person.
A hash of the key that is used in place of the key.
why: Modes such as CBC use this value so identical messages do not always produce identical ciphertext.
example: A file vault chooses a fresh starting value for each memo so two copies of the same memo encrypt differently.
scenario: Two identical messages encrypted with the same key must not produce the same ciphertext. What extra non-secret value is needed?
scenarioWrongs: The same starting block every time
A hash of the public key only
A zero block reused for every file
scenarioWhy: A new initialization vector changes the ciphertext even when the key and plaintext stay the same.

definition: Encryption that hides the data and also produces a tag that detects tampering with the ciphertext.
wrongs: Encryption that hides data but provides no check against changes to the ciphertext.
An unkeyed hash with no encryption of the message.
A certificate field that only stores a subject's name.
why: Constructions such as GCM encrypt the plaintext and create an authentication tag together.
example: A tunnel uses AES-GCM so a packet that was edited in transit fails its tag check and is dropped.
scenario: A link must hide packet contents and reject packets that are edited on the way. Which construction fits?
scenarioWrongs: An unkeyed checksum with no secret
A public digest of the plaintext only
scenarioWhy: Authenticated encryption supplies secrecy and a tag that reveals tampering.

definition: A cryptographic hash in the SHA-2 family that produces a 256-bit digest of its input.
wrongs: A symmetric cipher that encrypts data with a 256-bit key.
A public-key signature method that uses a 256-bit modulus as a cipher.
A tunneling protocol that sends traffic over port 256.
why: SHA-256 maps any input to a 256-bit digest and is widely used for integrity checks.
example: A package mirror prints a SHA-256 digest beside each download so students can verify the file.
scenario: A release process needs a 256-bit one-way fingerprint of a binary, not encryption. Which function fits?
scenarioWrongs: RSA used as a bulk cipher
scenarioWhy: SHA-256 is a hash function, and its output is a 256-bit digest.

definition: A message authentication code constructed from a cryptographic hash and a secret key.
wrongs: An unkeyed hash of a file name.
An extension field inside a public certificate.
A firewall action that blocks every hashed packet.
why: The secret key is mixed into the hash computation so an outsider cannot forge the tag.
example: A webhook checks a header by recomputing a keyed hash of the body with the shared secret.
scenario: An API already has SHA-256 and a shared secret and must authenticate request bodies. Which construction matches?
scenarioWrongs: A bare SHA-256 with no key
RSA encryption of the entire body
scenarioWhy: HMAC is the standard way to build a keyed tag from a hash function and a secret.

definition: Declaring a certificate untrustworthy before its printed expiration date.
wrongs: Extending a certificate so that it never expires.
Encrypting a certificate with a block cipher for storage.
Turning a certificate into a symmetric encryption key.
why: Revocation covers keys that were exposed, lost, or issued by mistake while the dates still look valid.
example: After a laptop holding a client certificate is stolen, the campus authority revokes that certificate the same day.
scenario: A private key on a lost laptop may be misused, and the certificate dates are still valid. What should the authority do?
scenarioWrongs: Extend it for five more years
scenarioWhy: Revocation tells relying parties to stop trusting the certificate before it expires.

definition: A suite that can authenticate and encrypt IP packets between hosts or security gateways.
wrongs: A file-hash format used only to check downloads in a browser.
A method that stores salted password hashes in a database.
An application format used to describe web pages.
why: IPsec protects traffic at the IP layer using security associations and protocols such as ESP.
example: Two branch routers maintain an IPsec tunnel so traffic between the offices is encrypted on the internet.
scenario: Two site routers must encrypt IP packets between their networks, not only web traffic. Which suite fits?
scenarioWhy: IPsec protects IP packets between gateways and therefore covers many applications.

definition: Firewall behavior that remembers connection state and allows return traffic belonging to an existing flow.
wrongs: Firewall behavior that judges every packet alone and never remembers a connection.
Encryption that chooses a brand-new key for every byte.
Hashing that keeps only the first packet of a flow.
why: The firewall records the connection and then accepts packets that match that remembered state.
example: A firewall allows an outbound web request and then permits the matching replies without a separate inbound allow rule.
scenario: Replies to connections a host started should pass, while unexpected inbound connections stay blocked. Which firewall behavior is that?
scenarioWrongs: Replacing the connection with a hash
scenarioWhy: Stateful inspection remembers legitimate connections and permits their return traffic.

definition: An inline control that detects suspected attacks and blocks the matching traffic.
wrongs: A sensor that only notifies an analyst and never drops traffic.
A cipher that hides payloads but does not look for attacks.
A certificate that stops a key pair from being created.
why: Unlike a detection-only monitor, this control sits in the traffic path so it can stop the activity.
example: An inline campus device drops connections that match a known attack signature before they reach a server.
scenario: A device in the traffic path must stop a matching attack at once, not merely record it. What role is it filling?
scenarioWrongs: A passive copy of the traffic
scenarioWhy: An intrusion prevention system can block traffic it classifies as an attack.

definition: A strategy that uses several independent controls so one failure does not fully expose the system.
wrongs: A strategy that relies on one shared password for every layer.
A strategy that turns off logging once a firewall is installed.
A strategy that encrypts disks and then removes all access checks.
why: Independent layers, such as network filtering, authentication, and encryption, cover different failures.
example: A records system sits behind a firewall, requires a second login factor, and encrypts the database disk.
scenario: Architects refuse to trust the firewall alone and also require login checks and encrypted storage. Which strategy is that?
scenarioWhy: Defense in depth stacks separate controls so bypassing one of them is not enough.

definition: The principle that each account or process gets only the access its task requires.
wrongs: The principle that every user receives administrator rights for convenience.
The principle that encryption keys should be published to all staff.
The principle that firewalls should allow every port by default.
why: Narrow rights limit the damage if that account is misused or taken over.
example: A backup account can read the archive share but cannot edit grades or create administrators.
scenario: A print service only needs to write to the print queue. Which principle says it should not be an administrator?
scenarioWrongs: Give every service full administrator rights
Publish the service key to all users
Allow every network port by default
scenarioWhy: Least privilege limits the print account to the access its job actually needs.

definition: A screened network segment that holds public-facing services apart from the internal network.
wrongs: The private segment where payroll systems sit with no extra boundary.
A client program that encrypts one laptop's disk.
A hash algorithm applied to public web pages.
why: Services in that segment can be reached from outside while stricter rules protect internal systems.
example: The university web server sits on a screened segment, and the firewall blocks it from opening connections to the student database.
scenario: A public website must be reachable from the internet but must not share a segment with payroll systems. Where should it be placed?
scenarioWrongs: On the same host as the student database
scenarioWhy: A DMZ separates public-facing hosts from sensitive internal systems.

definition: Encryption in which only the communicating endpoints can read the content, not the servers that forward it.
wrongs: Encryption that stops at the first proxy, which can read and then forward the content.
Hashing of packet headers performed by a router.
A logging feature that records ports but encrypts nothing.
why: Forwarding servers may see ciphertext, but they do not hold the keys needed to read the message.
example: A chat app encrypts messages on each phone so the provider's servers store ciphertext they cannot read.
scenario: Users want a chat provider to forward messages without being able to read them. Which protection fits?
scenarioWrongs: Encryption that the provider can decrypt
Hashing only the recipient's display name
scenarioWhy: End-to-end encryption leaves the readable message only on the users' endpoints.

definition: The processes for creating, distributing, storing, rotating, and retiring cryptographic keys.
wrongs: The process of choosing which firewall ports to open.
The process of writing user help pages for a website.
The process of compressing old logs after an incident.
why: Even a strong cipher fails if its keys are generated poorly, leaked, or never changed.
example: A clinic rotates database encryption keys each year and keeps the previous key only to read old backups.
scenario: A team selected AES but has no process for issuing, storing, or retiring keys. Which discipline is missing?
scenarioWhy: Key management covers the life cycle of the keys the cipher depends on.

definition: Public-key cryptography based on the difficulty of the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problem.
wrongs: A symmetric block cipher that encrypts 128-bit blocks.
A hash function whose digest is 160 bits long.
A packet filter that groups traffic by graph shape.
why: Elliptic-curve schemes provide public-key security with shorter keys than RSA at a similar strength.
example: A mobile app uses an elliptic-curve key pair so its certificates stay small on the phone.
scenario: A small device needs public-key security with shorter keys than a typical RSA modulus. Which approach fits?
scenarioWrongs: A short key in ECB mode
scenarioWhy: Elliptic-curve public-key schemes reach strong security with comparatively short keys.

definition: An exchange in which the verifier sends a fresh challenge and checks the prover's computed reply.
wrongs: An exchange in which the user repeats a static password blob with no new challenge.
A firewall step that only counts how many packets arrived.
A method that sends the private key itself as the reply.
why: A fresh challenge means an old captured reply will not match the next exchange.
example: A door reader sends a random challenge, and a smart card returns a signed reply that the reader checks.
scenario: A door reader must make yesterday's captured unlock message useless today. Which authentication pattern helps?
scenarioAnswer: A fresh challenge and a checked response
scenarioWrongs: Sending the private key in the clear
scenarioWhy: A new challenge binds the reply to this attempt, so a replayed old reply fails.

definition: A network authentication system that uses a trusted ticket service and time-limited tickets.
wrongs: A symmetric cipher used only to encrypt laptop disks.
A hash function designed for storing passwords.
A protocol that assigns network addresses to hosts.
why: A user authenticates to the trusted service and then presents tickets to application servers.
example: A campus domain uses Kerberos so a student signs in once and then opens file shares with tickets.
scenario: A domain needs single sign-on with time-limited tickets from a trusted service. Which system matches?
scenarioWhy: Kerberos issues time-limited tickets after authentication by a trusted service.

definition: An access model that grants permissions to roles and then assigns people to those roles.
wrongs: An access model that gives every person the same administrator rights.
An encryption mode that grants access by hashing the file name.
A routing model that assigns rights according to packet size.
why: Rights stay attached to the role, so a job change is handled by changing role membership.
example: A registrar gives instructors a grade-editor role and gives advisers a view-only role.
scenario: When a clerk becomes a supervisor, access should change by moving the person between job roles. Which model is that?
scenarioWrongs: One shared account for the whole office
Access chosen only by hardware address
Rights stored inside the password hash
scenarioWhy: Role-based access control attaches permissions to roles instead of copying them onto each person.

definition: Authentication that requires proof from at least two different categories of evidence.
wrongs: Authentication that asks for the same password on two successive screens.
Authentication that uses two user names and no secret.
Authentication that replaces the password with a hash of the user name.
why: The factors come from different categories, such as a secret, a device, or a biometric.
example: A payroll site requires both a password and a one-time code from a phone app.
scenario: A policy says a password alone is not enough for payroll and a phone code is also required. What control is that?
scenarioWhy: A password and a phone code are two different kinds of authentication evidence.

definition: Dividing a network into zones so traffic between those zones can be limited.
wrongs: Placing every server on one flat network with no internal boundaries.
Encrypting a single file without changing the network design.
Hashing switch settings and storing the digest off site.
why: Separate zones limit how far a problem on one part of the network can spread.
example: A college puts lab instruments on a segment that cannot open connections to the finance segment.
scenario: A compromised lab machine must still be unable to reach finance servers directly. Which design goal is that?
scenarioWrongs: One flat network for every system
One administrator password for both zones
scenarioWhy: Segmentation puts the lab and finance systems in zones with controlled paths between them.

definition: The security goal that authorized users can reach systems and data when they need them.
wrongs: The goal of keeping message contents secret from unauthorized readers.
The goal of proving that a sender cannot deny a signature.
The goal of mapping every file to a short digest.
why: Availability completes the confidentiality-integrity-availability triad by focusing on reliable access.
example: A campus directory uses a second server so lookups continue when one server is down for maintenance.
scenario: During maintenance, an exam site must stay reachable for students who are allowed to use it. Which goal is that?
scenarioWhy: Keeping an authorized service usable when it is needed is availability.

definition: A number used once so that a captured authentication or encryption message cannot be reused successfully.
wrongs: A key that is reused for every message during a year.
A certificate whose validity period never ends.
A counter that tells a firewall to accept duplicate handshakes.
why: Because the value is fresh, a message captured earlier will not match the current exchange.
example: A login server sends a new random number, and the client includes that number in its signed reply.
scenario: A login protocol must make a captured reply useless on the next attempt. Which value should change every time?
scenarioWhy: A new nonce ties the reply to the current attempt, so a replay fails.

definition: The hash property that it is infeasible to find two different inputs with the same digest.
wrongs: The property that a hash can be inverted to recover its exact input.
The property that every short file is stored unchanged inside the digest.
The property that two different ciphers always emit the same ciphertext.
why: Signatures and integrity checks fail if an attacker can swap in a second input with the same digest.
example: A contract system relies on collision resistance so a different contract cannot be found with the same digest.
scenario: A signature covers the hash of a contract. Which hash property stops someone from swapping in a different contract with that same hash?
scenarioWhy: Collision resistance makes it infeasible to find a second contract that hashes to the signed digest.

definition: Attaching a digital signature to software so users can check its publisher and whether it was altered.
wrongs: Compressing software so that it downloads in less time.
Publishing source code with an unsigned checksum and no publisher key.
Encrypting a program so the operating system is unable to start it.
why: The signature covers the software bytes, and the publisher certificate identifies who signed them.
example: An operating system warns about an unsigned installer but runs a campus app that carries a trusted signature.
scenario: Students should detect a changed lab installer and see which department published it. What should the department attach?
scenarioWrongs: An unsigned checksum with no publisher key
scenarioWhy: Code signing binds the installer bytes to the department's certified signing key.
